text: A one-page website for Brew Lab, a specialty coffee shop in Indiranagar, Bengaluru: menu with prices, opening hours, location, pre-order a coffee for pickup, a section about our beans and farms, and a loyalty card explainer (buy 9, get the 10th free).

@CEO the brief leaves three choices open that change risk and external commitments. Everything the brief lists stays in scope: menu with prices, hours, location, pre-order for pickup, beans and farms, loyalty explainer. Please decide each below.
1. How should a pre-order reach the shop, given the site is one static file with no server?
   Option 1: Order summary plus a call button: the page builds the order and the customer phones the shop to place it. Simplest and no third-party data. Risk: it is not really pre-ordering, and it adds phone load at peak hours.
   Option 2: Prefilled WhatsApp message: the customer builds an order on the page and it opens WhatsApp to the shop's number with the order text. Works with no backend and staff already read WhatsApp. Risk: the order is not confirmed until staff reply, and it needs a real shop number.
   Option 3: Hosted form service (such as Formspree or Google Forms) that emails or logs each order. Gives a record outside a chat app. Risk: a third party holds customer names and phone numbers, and staff must watch an inbox, so orders can be missed.
2. How should the customer pay for a pre-order?
   Option 1: Pay at pickup, with a pickup time slot chosen at order time so the shop can plan. Reduces rush surprises. Risk: slots promise a ready time the shop must keep, and the shop must give its real capacity per slot.
   Option 2: Pay at pickup only. Keeps the site free of payment handling and legal exposure. Risk: no-shows leave made drinks unpaid and wasted.
   Option 3: Online payment at order time through a hosted gateway such as Razorpay payment links. Reduces no-shows. Risk: it needs a Razorpay account and credentials from the shop, adds compliance and refund duties, and a single static file cannot confirm payment reliably.
3. Where do the real facts come from (prices, hours, address, map pin, bean origins and farm names, shop phone or WhatsApp number)?
   Option 1: Build now with plausible invented details for Indiranagar, such as sample prices and farms. The page looks complete. Risk: customers could be misled on prices, hours and sourcing claims, and the farm story could be false.
   Option 2: Hold the build until the Requester supplies every fact. No wrong data can go live. Risk: the run pauses and nothing is built until they reply.
   Option 3: Build now with clearly marked placeholder values, such as a visible 'TBC' tag, and have the Requester confirm before the site is called done. Progress continues. Risk: a placeholder price or hour could reach customers if the final check is skipped.

@Identity decisions below, Adaptation should build to these. The brief was silent on all three, so I chose on the merits. Trade-off accepted: pre-orders are requests until staff reply, and the page ships with visible TBC placeholders that the Requester must fill in before go-live.
1. How should a pre-order reach the shop, given the site is one static file with no server? Prefilled WhatsApp message: the customer builds an order on the page and it opens WhatsApp to the shop's number with the order text. Works with no backend and staff already read WhatsApp. Risk: the order is not confirmed until staff reply, and it needs a real shop number. (WhatsApp needs no backend or third-party data store, staff already use it, and it is a real pre-order unlike a phone call.)
2. How should the customer pay for a pre-order? Pay at pickup, with a pickup time slot chosen at order time so the shop can plan. Reduces rush surprises. Risk: slots promise a ready time the shop must keep, and the shop must give its real capacity per slot. (Pay at pickup avoids payment compliance a static file cannot support, and a chosen pickup slot, labelled as a request until staff confirm on WhatsApp, limits rush surprises and no-show waste without promising capacity the page cannot enforce.)
3. Where do the real facts come from (prices, hours, address, map pin, bean origins and farm names, shop phone or WhatsApp number)? Build now with clearly marked placeholder values, such as a visible 'TBC' tag, and have the Requester confirm before the site is called done. Progress continues. Risk: a placeholder price or hour could reach customers if the final check is skipped. (Visible TBC placeholders keep the build moving without inventing prices, hours or farm claims, and the open facts are tracked as Requester inputs that do not block done.)

@Adaptation charter recorded. All six brief items stay in scope. Build to the CEO's decisions: WhatsApp pre-order, pay at pickup with a requested pickup slot, and visible TBC for every fact we do not have. Propose the first workflow.
@Adaptation Charter valid: statement present, 10 checkable done-when items. Work can start.

@Priority two workflows, 45 of 50. WF1 creates the single file with the menu and the WhatsApp pre-order. WF2 adds hours and location together, plus beans and farms and the loyalty card together. Merging sections is the shortcut that fits the budget, and it leaves no room for separate styling. Every unknown fact is a visible TBC tag.

proposal.name: Single file with menu and WhatsApp pre-order
proposal.goal_gap: No site file exists. The menu and the pre-order flow are missing.
proposal.expected_outcome: One HTML file with inline CSS and JS and no backend. It has a menu section listing drinks with a price or a TBC tag. It has a pre-order form where the customer picks items and quantities, enters a name and chooses a pickup slot labelled as a request. A button opens a WhatsApp link with the order text prefilled. The number is a visible TBC placeholder. The page states payment is at pickup and the order is a request until staff confirm on WhatsApp. It has no payment or card-entry fields and stores no data.
proposal.completion_check: The file opens with no build step and contains a menu section with each price in rupees or a TBC tag. The pre-order form has item quantity, name and pickup slot inputs. The button's link is a wa.me URL with encoded order text and a TBC number. The page states pay at pickup and request until staff confirm. The file contains no payment or card inputs and no invented prices or numbers.

proposal.name: Hours and location, beans and farms, loyalty card
proposal.goal_gap: The file has no hours, location, sourcing or loyalty content.
proposal.expected_outcome: The same file gains a Visit section with its own hours and location blocks. The hours cover all seven days with each unknown time shown as a TBC tag. The location block names Indiranagar, Bengaluru and shows the street address and map pin as TBC tags. It also gains a Beans and farms and Loyalty section. Every bean origin and farm name is a TBC tag and no sourcing claim is made. The loyalty block states buy 9 coffees, get the 10th free.
proposal.completion_check: The file has headed blocks for hours, location, beans and farms, and loyalty. Hours list Monday to Sunday with TBC or a time. The location text names Indiranagar, Bengaluru and the address and map pin are TBC tags. Beans and farms has only TBC tags for origins and farm names. The loyalty text reads buy 9 coffees, get the 10th free. No invented address, hours, farm name or phone number appears.
